text: The image of \([\gamma_2,\gamma_2]\) in \(\gamma_4/\gamma_5\) is spanned by the brackets \([L_2,L_2]\subseteq L_4\) of \(L=L(G)\), so it suffices to show \([L_2,L_2]=0\). If \(L_2\) is cyclic, the alternating bracket \(L_2\times L_2\to L_4\) vanishes. Otherwise \(pL_3=0\), hence \(pL_4=0\) (\(L_4=[L_3,L_1]\)), and dividing \(L\) by the ideal \(pL_1\oplus pL_2\oplus0\oplus H\oplus L_{\ge5}\), where \(H\subset L_4\) is a hyperplane missing a given nonzero bracket \([u,v]\), we get a graded \(\mathbb F_p\)-Lie algebra \(M=M_1\oplus\dots\oplus M_4\) generated by \(M_1\) with \(\dim M_2=2\), \(\dim M_3=\dim M_4=1\) and \([M_2,M_2]\ne0\). text: Write \([z,z']=\omega(z,z')w\) for \(z,z'\in M_2\), \(M_4=\langle w\rangle\), \(M_3=\langle t\rangle\), \([x,t]=\varphi(x)w\), \([x,z]=\beta(x,z)t\) and \([x,y]=\alpha(x,y)\) for \(x,y\in M_1\), \(z\in M_2\). A nonzero alternating form on a plane is nondegenerate, so \(\omega\) is; \(\varphi\ne0\) since \(M_4=[M_1,M_3]\). Pick \(e\) with \(\varphi(e)=1\) and let \(K=\ker\varphi\). The Jacobi identity for \(x,y\in M_1\), \(z\in M_2\) reads \[\omega(\alpha(x,y),z)=\varphi(x)\beta(y,z)-\varphi(y)\beta(x,z).\] For \(x,y\in K\) the right side vanishes, so \(\alpha(K,K)=0\) and \(M_2=\alpha(e,K)\); for \(x=e\), \(y=k\in K\) it gives \(\beta(k,z)=\omega(\alpha(e,k),z)\). The Jacobi identity for \(e,k_1,k_2\in K\), with \(u_i=\alpha(e,k_i)\) and \(\alpha(k_1,k_2)=0\), gives \(\beta(k_1,u_2)-\beta(k_2,u_1)=0\), i.e. \(2\,\omega(u_1,u_2)=0\). As \(p\ne2\) and the \(u_i\) run over \(M_2\), \(\omega=0\), a contradiction.

Since \(\Lambda^2(C_{3^a}\times C_3^{s-1})\) has exponent \(3\), the factors \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(\gamma_4\) are still elementary abelian, so identities (i)–(iii) of the proof of Theorem 6.6 hold for all \(x\in Q\), and moreover \([x^{3^n},y]=[x,y]^{3^n}\) for \(n\ge2\). The class \(x_s^{3^a}\gamma_3\) does not depend on the choice of \(x_s\), so there are two cases. If \(x_s^{3^a}\notin\gamma_3\), Tahara's (B) forces \(3\mid u_{is}\), every term involving \(x_s^{3^a}\) vanishes by the identity above, and the proof of Theorem 6.6 goes through. If \(x_s^{3^a}\in\gamma_3\), the coefficients \(u_{is}\) are unrestricted. For \(a\ge3\) all new terms are \(3^a\)-th powers of elements of \(\gamma_3\) and vanish. For \(a=2\), (E) now gives \(\sum_i[x_i^3,r_i]=-\sum_iu_{is}[x_i,x_s]^9\), so the pairing \(\tfrac12\sum_i[x_i^3,r_i]\) cancels, formally, only half of the new term \(\sum_iu_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]\) of \(g\); the remainder is \(\tfrac12[r_s^3,x_s]\) with \(r_s=\prod_ix_i^{3u_{is}}\), and condition (E) for the row \(s\), which sees \(u_{is}\) through (B) with \(d(s)/d(i)=3\), gives \(r_s^3\in\gamma_4\). So \(g=1\) for every admissible family. (This step is not void: a computation finds groups of order \(3^{16}\) with \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\) and \([x_i^9,x_s]\ne1\).) Here \(\alpha^{(ss)}=0\) is read off Tahara's generators of types (V), (VI) [Tah81, pp. 150–151].
